summary: Defines a MIB with the elements common to monitoring any network service application. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: A network service is a program that offers a service over a network, such as a mail server or a directory. This RFC defines a standard set of SNMP values that describe any such program: its name, whether it is up, how many clients are connected, and when it last changed state. A MIB for one particular service can build on top of it.

questions: how to monitor a network service with snmp
what is the network services monitoring mib
how do i monitor a mail server with snmp
subtitle: A common SNMP table that lets one tool see whether any network service is up and who is connected to it.

tldr.problem: Network management tools work on the layers below the application, and there was no standard way to ask an application itself how it is doing. The difficulty grows as applications become more complex.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an SMIv2 MIB module with two tables: one row per network service application on the system, and one row per active association to those applications. The rows hold the application's name, version, operational state, and counts of current, accumulated, rejected and failed associations.
tldr.outcome: Any network service can be watched with the same objects, and service-specific MIBs can build on top. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2248 and is read-only throughout.

facts.label: applOperStatus values
facts.value: up, down, halted, congested, restarting, quiescing

today: RFC 2788 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2000. It obsoletes RFC 2248, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Module Covers
sections.content:
A networked application is a realization of some well-defined service on one or more host computers that is accessible via some network, uses some network for its internal operations, or both. The RFC defines a MIB containing the elements common to the monitoring of any network service application. That information includes a table of all monitorable network service applications, a count of the associations to each application, and basic information about the parameters and status of each application-related association.

The MIB may be used on its own for any application, and for most simple applications this suffices. It is also designed to serve as a building block used together with application-specific monitoring and management, such as MIBs defining additional variables for monitoring a Message Transfer Agent service or a Directory Service Agent service. The RFC expects further MIBs of this nature to be specified.

The MIB does not attempt to provide facilities for management of the host or hosts the network service application runs on, nor does it provide facilities for monitoring applications that provide something other than a network service. Host resource and general application monitoring is handled by either the Host Resources MIB (RFC 1514) or the application MIB (RFC 2287).

Section 1 places the module inside the SNMP Network Management Framework, whose five major components are an overall architecture (RFC 2571), the SMIv1 and SMIv2 mechanisms for describing and naming objects, the SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3 message protocols, the protocol operations for accessing management information in STD 15 and RFC 1905, and the fundamental applications of RFC 2573 with the view-based access control mechanism of RFC 2575.

The memo specifies a MIB module compliant to SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the resulting translated MIB must be semantically equivalent except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, namely the use of Counter64.
sections.plainLanguage: A network service is a program that offers a service over a network, such as a mail server or a directory. This RFC defines a standard set of SNMP values that describe any such program: its name, whether it is up, how many clients are connected, and when it last changed state. A MIB for one particular service can build on top of it.

sections.title: Why a Common Monitoring MIB
sections.content:
Much effort has been expended on tools to manage lower layer network facilities, but relatively little on managing application layer entities. The RFC argues that it is neither efficient nor reasonable to manage all aspects of application layer entities using only lower layer information, and that the difficulty of doing so increases dramatically as application entities become more complex.

This leads to a substantial need to monitor applications that provide network services, particularly distributed components such as MTAs and DSAs, by monitoring specific aspects of the application itself. The reasons to monitor such components include, but are not limited to, measuring load, detecting broken connectivity, isolating system failures and locating congestion.

Two requirements follow. It must be possible to monitor a large number of components, which is typical for a large organization, and application monitoring must be integrated into general network management. The specification defines simple read-only access, which is sufficient to determine up or down status and to give an indication of a broad class of operational problems.

Section 2.1 sets the relationship to other MIBs. This MIB is intended to provide only the facilities common to the monitoring of any network service application, and not all the facilities needed to monitor any specific application. Each specific type of network service application is expected to have a MIB of its own that makes use of these common facilities.
sections.plainLanguage: Most management tools look at the network below the application, and there is no standard way to ask an application itself how it is doing. The RFC argues that this matters for large distributed components, such as mail transfer agents and directory agents, where the reasons to watch include measuring load, spotting broken connections, isolating failures and finding congestion.

sections.title: What the MIB Deliberately Leaves Out
sections.content:
The RFC states that the framework it provides is very minimal, and that there is a lot more that could be done. It lists four examples of what is left out.

  • General network service application configuration monitoring and control.
  • Detailed examination and modification of individual entries in service-specific request queues.
  • Probing to determine the status of a specific request, for example the location of a mail message with a specific message-id.
  • Requesting that certain actions be performed, for example forcing an immediate connection and transfer of pending messages to some specific system.

All these capabilities are, in the RFC's words, both impressive and useful. However, they would require provisions for strict security checking, and they would also mandate a much more complex design with many characteristics likely to be fairly implementation-specific. As a result, such facilities are likely to be both contentious and difficult to implement. The document keeps things simple and focuses on the basic monitoring aspect of managing applications providing network services, with the goal of providing a framework that is simple, useful and widely implementable.

Section 2.3 adds that the MIB attempts to provide information about the operational aspects of an application, while further information about the actual configuration of a given application may be kept in other places. The applDirectoryName or applURL objects may be used to point to where such information is kept.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC deliberately keeps the MIB small. It does not offer configuration control, does not let you inspect or change individual entries in service-specific queues, does not let you ask where a particular message has got to, and does not let you trigger actions such as forcing an immediate transfer of pending messages. Each of those would need strict security checks and a much more complex design, and the RFC judges them contentious and hard to implement.

sections.title: Application Objects
sections.content:
The MIB defines a set of general purpose attributes appropriate for a range of applications that provide network services, and both OSI and non-OSI services can be accommodated. Additional tables defined in extensions to this MIB provide attributes specific to specific network services.

Two tables are defined. The first has one row for each operational network service application on the system. The only static information held on the application is its name; all other static information should be obtained from various directory services. The applDirectoryName is an external key, which allows an SNMP MIB entry to be cleanly related to the X.500 Directory. In SNMP terms the applications are grouped in a table called applTable, indexed by an integer key applIndex.

The type of the application will be determined by one or both of two things: additional MIB variables specific to the applications, and an association to the application of a specific protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The module has two tables. The first has one row for each network service application on the system and is indexed by an integer. The second has one row for each open connection to those applications. The type of an application is worked out from the extra MIB variables defined for it, from the protocol the connection uses, or from both.

sections.title: The Two Tables in Detail
sections.content:
The module is named application and is placed at mib-2 27. The applTable holds objects applying to all kinds of applications providing network services, and each monitorable application should have a single entry. Its index applIndex is an integer in the range 1 to 2147483647 and is used for the lexicographic ordering of the table.

The row holds applName, the name the application chooses to be known by, and applDirectoryName, the Distinguished Name of the directory entry where static information about the application is stored, where an empty string indicates that no information about the application is available in the directory. There is also applVersion, usually defined by the vendor of the software, and applUptime, the value of sysUpTime when the application was last initialized. applDescription is a text description and applURL a URL pointing to a description, both intended for a status display.

applOperStatus gives the operational status as one of six values: up, meaning the service is operational and available; down, meaning it is not available; halted, meaning it is operational but not available; congested, meaning it is operational but no additional inbound associations can be accommodated; restarting, meaning it is currently unavailable but in the process of restarting and will be available soon; and quiescing, meaning the service is operational but in the process of shutting down, and additional inbound associations may be rejected. applLastChange is the value of sysUpTime when the application entered its current operational state.

Five objects count associations. applInboundAssociations and applOutboundAssociations are gauges for the current number of connections where the application is the responder and where it is the initiator. applAccumulatedInboundAssociations and applAccumulatedOutboundAssociations are counters for the totals since application initialization. applRejectedInboundAssociations counts inbound associations the application itself has rejected, and the RFC warns that it does not count rejections at lower layers of the network, so it may not reflect the true number of failed inbound associations. applFailedOutboundAssociations counts associations where the application was the initiator and establishment failed. applLastInboundActivity and applLastOutboundActivity record when the application last had an association in each direction.

The assocTable augments that information with a set of all active application associations, and is indexed by applIndex together with an assocIndex integer in the same 1 to 2147483647 range. Each row holds assocRemoteApplication, the name of the system running the remote application, which for an IP-based application should be a domain name or IP address and for an OSI application the string encoded distinguished name of the managed object. It holds assocApplicationProtocol, an identification of the protocol used, which for an OSI application is the Application Context and for Internet applications takes the form {applTCPProtoID port} or {applUDPProtoID port} with the primary port number of the protocol. It holds assocApplicationType, one of uainitiator, uaresponder, peerinitiator and peerresponder, indicating whether the remote application is a client or a peer, and whether the remote end initiated the connection or responded to one the local application made. MTAs and messaging gateways are considered peers for this purpose. Finally it holds assocDuration, the value of sysUpTime when the association started.
sections.plainLanguage: The first table holds the name of the application, its version, when it was last started, its operational state, how many connections it has open in each direction, how many it has had since it started, and counters for the connections it rejected or that failed. The second table holds, for each open connection, the name of the remote system, the protocol, whether the remote end is a client or a peer, and when the connection started.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2248
sections.content:
Section 5 of the RFC states that this revision corrects a few minor technical errors in the construction of the network services MIB in RFC 2248. In addition, the applName, applVersion and applDescription fields have been changed from DisplayStrings to SnmpAdminStrings.

The reference to RFC 1779 has also been updated to RFC 2253, which in turn adds the ability for distinguished names to be in the UTF-8 character set. The module's own revision history records that the RFC 2788 revision changes a number of DisplayStrings to SnmpAdminStrings, and notes that this change is not strictly supported by SMIv2. The alternative of deprecating the old objects and defining new ones would have a more adverse impact on backward compatibility and interoperability, given the particular semantics of these objects.

The conformance statements show the same history. The RFC 1565 compliance statements and groups are marked obsolete, the RFC 2248 ones are marked deprecated, and the current ones are applRFC2788Compliance and assocRFC2788Compliance, with the groups applRFC2788Group and assocRFC2788Group. The RFC notes that the RFC 2788 group adds the applDirectoryName object that was missing in RFC 2248.
sections.plainLanguage: This version fixes a few small errors in the previous one and changes three text fields from one type to another. It also updates the reference for distinguished names, which adds the ability to use the UTF-8 character set in those names.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that there are no management objects defined in this MIB that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. So, if the MIB is implemented correctly, there is no risk that an intruder can alter or create any of its management objects through direct SNMP SET operations.

However, the MIB does provide passive information about the existence, type and configuration of applications on a given host, which could potentially indicate some sort of vulnerability. The information the MIB provides about network usage could also be used to analyze network traffic patterns.

The RFC adds that SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to access and read, change, create or delete the objects in this MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing in this MIB can be written: every object is read-only, so an intruder cannot change or create any of it with an SNMP write. The RFC notes that reading it still reveals which applications exist on a host, and that the usage figures could be used to analyse traffic patterns. It also notes that SNMPv1 on its own is not a secure environment.
